## 1. Introduction

```{=html}
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic autoimmune liver disease in which the small bile ducts are progressively destroyed, eventually leading to cirrhosis and liver failure. This analysis uses data from the Mayo Clinic randomised placebo-controlled trial of D-penicillamine, conducted between 1974 and 1984 and distributed with the R `survival` package.

The aims were to (1) compare time to death or liver transplant between the treatment groups using Kaplan-Meier estimation and the log-rank test, and (2) identify prognostic factors using a Cox proportional hazards model including treatment, age, sex, bilirubin and albumin.
```

## 2. Setup

```{r}
library(survival)
```

## 3. Data preparation

```{r}
pbc_trial <- subset(pbc, !is.na(trt))

pbc_trial$event <- as.integer(pbc_trial$status >= 1)

pbc_trial$trt <- factor(pbc_trial$trt,
                        levels = c(1, 2),
                        labels = c("D-penicillamine", "Placebo"))

pbc_trial$time_years <- pbc_trial$time / 365.25

```

We restricted the analysis to the 312 patients who took part in the randomised trial, excluding 106 non-randomised patients with no treatment assignment. The outcome is a composite of death or liver transplant: 144 patients experienced the event (125 deaths and 19 transplants), and 168 were censored. Follow-up time was converted from days to years.

## 4. Kaplan-Meier survival curves

```{r}
km_fit <- survfit(Surv(time_years, event) ~ trt, data = pbc_trial)

km_fit

plot(km_fit,
     col = c("steelblue", "darkorange"),
     lwd = 2,
     mark.time = TRUE,
     xlab = "Years since registration",
     ylab = "Probability of no death or transplant")
legend("bottomleft",
       legend = levels(pbc_trial$trt),
       col = c("steelblue", "darkorange"),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n")

survdiff(Surv(time_years, event) ~ trt, data = pbc_trial)

```

```{=html}
The Kaplan-Meier curves for the two treatment groups overlap throughout follow-up and cross several times. Median time to death or transplant was 7.1 years (95% CI 6.4–11.2) in the D-penicillamine group and 8.7 years (95% CI 7.7–10.5) in the placebo group, with widely overlapping confidence intervals. The log-rank test showed no evidence of a difference between groups (χ² = 0.1, df = 1, p = 0.7). Estimates beyond about 10 years are less reliable because few patients remained at risk.
```

## 5. Cox proportional hazards model

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(pbc_trial$bili, main = "Bilirubin", xlab = "mg/dL")
hist(log2(pbc_trial$bili), main = "log2(Bilirubin)", xlab = "log2(mg/dL)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))   
```

```{r}
cox_fit <- coxph(Surv(time_years, event) ~ trt + age + sex + log2(bili) + albumin,
                 data = pbc_trial)
summary(cox_fit)
```

```{=html}
Bilirubin was strongly right-skewed, so it was entered on the log2 scale; hazard ratios for bilirubin therefore refer to a doubling of its value.
After adjustment, treatment was not associated with the hazard of death or transplant (HR for placebo vs D-penicillamine 1.07, 95% CI 0.77–1.50, p = 0.69), consistent with the log-rank test. Bilirubin was the strongest predictor: each doubling was associated with a near two-fold increase in hazard (HR 1.95, 95% CI 1.72–2.20). Higher albumin was protective (HR 0.33 per 1 g/dL, 95% CI 0.22–0.50), and older age was associated with higher hazard (HR 1.02 per year, 95% CI 1.00–1.04; roughly 21% per decade). The hazard was lower in women, but this was not statistically significant (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.45–1.12), possibly reflecting the small number of men in the trial. The model showed good discrimination (concordance 0.82).
```

## 6. Checking the proportional hazards assumption

```{r}
ph_test <- cox.zph(cox_fit)
ph_test
```

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (i in 1:5) {
  plot(ph_test[i])
  abline(h = coef(cox_fit)[i], col = "red", lty = 2)
}
```
The proportional hazards assumption was assessed using scaled Schoenfeld residuals. There was no evidence of violation for any covariate (all p > 0.15) or globally (p = 0.59). The smoothed residual plots were broadly flat for all covariates; the albumin curve suggested a slight weakening of its protective effect later in follow-up, but this was not statistically significant (p = 0.17). Wider confidence bands at later times reflect the smaller number of patients still at risk.

## 7. Discussion

```{=html}
### Main findings

D-penicillamine showed no benefit over placebo, either in the unadjusted Kaplan-Meier comparison or after adjustment for other covariates. In contrast, markers of liver function were strong prognostic factors: higher bilirubin and lower albumin were both associated with a substantially higher hazard of death or transplant, and older age was associated with a modest increase in hazard. The model discriminated well (concordance 0.82), and the proportional hazards assumption appeared reasonable.

### Limitations

- **Composite endpoint.** Death and transplant were combined into a single event. Transplant is a treatment decision rather than a disease outcome, and it prevents death from liver disease from being observed. A competing-risks approach (e.g. cause-specific hazards or Fine-Gray models) would separate the two outcomes.
- **Linearity.** Age, log2(bilirubin) and albumin were assumed to act linearly on the log-hazard; this was not formally checked (e.g. with martingale residuals or splines).
- **Small number of men**, which limits the precision of the sex effect.
- **Historical data.** The trial predates current treatment (ursodeoxycholic acid), so absolute risks may not apply to patients today.

### Next steps

The `pbcseq` dataset contains repeated biomarker measurements for the same patients. A natural extension is a joint model linking the longitudinal trajectory of bilirubin to the hazard of death or transplant.
```
